title: Effects of Eco-labels and Price Discounts on Promoting More Sustainable Grocery Purchases in an Online UK Supermarket: A Randomised Controlled Field Trial
abstract: A randomised controlled field trial investigating eco-labels and price discounts for environmentally sustainable food purchases in UK online grocery shopping. The study investigates whether labels, financial incentives and their combination can shift grocery decisions.
angle: Can a supermarket nudge shoppers towards greener baskets?
teaser: What happens when greener groceries become easier to spot—and cheaper to choose? A UK online supermarket field trial tests whether information, money, or a combination can shift what lands in our baskets.
image_alt: Colourful fruit and vegetable supermarket display
authors: Thijs van Rens, Helena Bentil, Peter Scarborough, Hamideh Mohtashami Borzadaran, Michael Clark, Claire Thompson, Jessica Brock, Elisa Becker, Laura Cornelsen, Martin White and Oyinlola Oyebode
venue: SSRN / Preprints with The Lancet (working paper)

title: Health economics evidence for food system policy: a systematic review of reviews
abstract: Thirty-six systematic reviews covered 718 primary studies. Twenty-one reviews addressed demand-side interventions, four supply-side alone, and eleven combinations. Supply-side approaches such as reformulation were more effective at changing dietary behaviours than demand-side measures such as labelling in the reviewed evidence. The authors recommend societal cost-benefit analysis and more investigation of effective policy packages.
angle: What actually works when governments try to improve our diets?
teaser: Taxes, labels, reformulation, subsidies: which tools really improve diets? A review spanning 718 studies suggests changing what companies sell may matter more than simply telling consumers what to buy.
image_alt: Fresh fruit and vegetables on a table
authors: Lin Fu, Irina Pokhilenko, Thijs van Rens, Richard Smith and Emma Frew

title: Why did we think wages are rigid for all those years?
abstract: Using U.S. Current Population Survey data, this study finds that rounding in workers' reported wages exaggerates the spike at zero nominal wage growth. Adjusting for rounding shrinks the apparent share of unchanged wages from 15–20% to 7–12%, consistent with recent administrative-data estimates.
angle: The wage freeze that wasn't quite what it seemed
teaser: Economists have spent decades puzzling over why wages seem so hard to cut. Part of the mystery may lie not in employers' pay policies, but in how workers round the numbers when surveys ask about their earnings.
image_alt: Calculator and financial paperwork on desk
authors: See-Yu Chan, Stephan Hobler and Thijs van Rens

title: Promoting environmentally sustainable food purchases in online grocery shopping: insights from a pilot randomised controlled field trial
abstract: The research team built a Chrome browser extension to deliver environmental eco-labels on a UK supermarket website. Of 504 screened, 161 were eligible and 57 installed the extension, with 22 shopping at least once. The study did not find a statistically significant difference in eco-scores of purchases, but established the feasibility of testing interventions without supermarket cooperation.
angle: Could a browser extension change the weekly food shop?
teaser: A small pilot put sustainability labels directly into a real online supermarket. The biggest discovery wasn't a dramatic change in buying—it was a new way to test shopping interventions without needing a retailer to take part.
authors: Helena Bentil, Oyinlola Oyebode, Peter Scarborough, Claire Thompson, Jessica Brock, Michael Clark, Martin White and Thijs van Rens
